(CNN) -- Cambodia and Thailand have agreed to redeploy some troops away from the site of a border temple at the center of a tense military standoff in its second week. Thai soldiers take a rest near the Preah Vihear temple in Preah Vihear province. The decision came after the two sides met to resolve the impasse. Government officials from both nations plan to meet again to decide how many troops will remain at the site of the Preah Vihear temple, the Thai News Agency reported Monday. At a later meeting, the two sides plan to discuss how to tackle the thorny issue at the center of the ongoing dispute -- the question of whether land around the temple belongs to Thailand or Cambodia. The 11th century temple sits atop a cliff on Cambodian soil but has its most accessible entrance on the Thai side. The two countries differ on whether some territory around the temple forms part of Thailand or Cambodia. The decision to redeploy troops took place after a Monday meeting in Siem Reap, Cambodia. Last week, an eight-hour meeting between Thai and Cambodian officials ended with both sides agreeing on only one point: that troops each country has amassed at the site of the temple will not fire on each other. The International Court of Justice awarded the temple to Cambodia in 1962. Thailand claims, however, that the 1.8 square mile (4.6 sq. km) area around it was never fully demarcated. Thailand says the dispute arose from the fact that the Cambodian government used a map drawn during the French occupation of Cambodia -- a map that places the temple and surrounding area in Cambodian territory. This month, the United Nations approved Cambodia's application to have the temple listed as a World Heritage Site -- a place the U.N. says has outstanding universal value. The decision re-ignited tensions, with some in Thailand fearing it will make it difficult for their country to lay claim to disputed land around the temple. Opposition parties in Thailand used the issue to attack the government, which initially backed the heritage listing. Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Sen, who has been in power since 1985, portrayed the U.N. recognition as a national triumph in the run-up to the general elections. Analysts believe that the nationalist sentiments stirred up by the military standoff helped Hun Sen's ruling party win enough seats in Sunday's parliamentary elections so that it can form a government without the need for a coalition. The current flare-up began July 15, when Cambodian guards briefly detained three Thais who crossed into the area. Once they were let go, the three refused to leave the territory. Cambodia claims Thailand sent troops to retrieve the trio and gradually built up their numbers. Thailand denies that, saying its troops are deployed in Thai territory.

**Military tensions flare around Preah Vihear temple as Thailand-Cambodia border dispute exposes deep political fault lines**

*By Staff Writer*

The ancient Hindu temple of Preah Vihear, perched on a cliff in the Dangrek Mountains overlooking the Cambodian plains, has long been more than an archaeological treasure. For decades, the 11th-century Khmer sanctuary has stood at the center of a volatile border dispute between Thailand and Cambodia—one that has repeatedly drawn troops, artillery and nationalist politics into a remote but symbolically charged stretch of frontier.

Although the International Court of Justice ruled in 1962 that the temple itself belongs to Cambodia, the surrounding land—especially several square kilometers near the temple entrance—has remained contested. That ambiguity has periodically turned the area into a flashpoint, with both countries accusing the other of encroachment, militarization and exploiting the dispute for domestic political gain.

## A temple with outsized national meaning

Preah Vihear was built during the Khmer Empire and is regarded by Cambodia as a major symbol of its ancient civilization. The temple sits atop a steep escarpment along the border, geographically more easily accessible from Thailand in some areas but historically and legally tied to Cambodia by international rulings.

The modern dispute stems from maps drawn during the French colonial period, when Cambodia was part of French Indochina and Thailand—then Siam—negotiated border arrangements with France. A key map placed Preah Vihear on the Cambodian side of the border. Thailand later argued that the map did not reflect the true watershed boundary and that the surrounding territory remained unsettled.

In 1962, the International Court of Justice ruled that Cambodia had sovereignty over the temple. Thailand complied by withdrawing from the temple area, but many Thais continued to view the ruling as unfair, particularly because the court did not fully settle the status of nearby land.

That unresolved area became the core of later confrontation.

## UNESCO listing reignites the dispute

The dispute intensified dramatically in 2008, when UNESCO listed Preah Vihear as a World Heritage Site. Cambodia celebrated the designation as international recognition of its cultural heritage. In Thailand, however, nationalist groups claimed the listing could weaken Thailand’s claim to adjacent territory.

The issue quickly became entangled in Thailand’s domestic political crisis. Anti-government activists accused Thai leaders of “selling out” national territory by appearing to support Cambodia’s UNESCO bid. Street protests and legal challenges followed, and the temple became a rallying point for nationalist sentiment.

Cambodia, led at the time by Prime Minister Hun Sen, accused Thailand of allowing domestic politics to obstruct a legitimate cultural listing. Thai officials argued that Cambodia’s management plan for the heritage site might imply sovereignty over disputed land.

What began as a heritage dispute escalated into a military standoff.

## Troop buildups and armed clashes

From 2008 onward, both Thailand and Cambodia deployed soldiers near the temple. The rugged terrain, limited visibility and overlapping claims created conditions for confrontation. Several armed clashes broke out over the next few years, causing casualties on both sides and forcing thousands of civilians in border villages to flee.

The most serious fighting occurred in 2011, when artillery and rocket fire were reported near Preah Vihear and at nearby disputed temple sites. Each government blamed the other for starting the clashes. Thailand said Cambodian troops had intruded into disputed areas; Cambodia accused Thailand of aggression and appealed for international intervention.

The fighting alarmed the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, which traditionally avoids involvement in member states’ territorial disputes. Indonesia, then ASEAN chair, attempted to mediate, and Cambodia sought support from the United Nations Security Council. Thailand preferred bilateral negotiations, wary of internationalizing the dispute.

The crisis exposed a broader diplomatic divide: Cambodia sought third-party involvement to restrain Thailand, while Thailand insisted the border issue should be resolved directly between the two governments.

## The 2013 ICJ clarification

In response to renewed tensions, Cambodia asked the International Court of Justice to clarify its 1962 judgment. In 2013, the court reaffirmed that Cambodia had sovereignty over the temple and ruled that Thailand must withdraw from a promontory surrounding it.

The decision reduced some legal ambiguity, but it did not settle the entire border. Both governments publicly accepted the ruling, and the situation around Preah Vihear became calmer. Still, the underlying sensitivities remain powerful. The border has not been fully demarcated in all areas, and nationalist groups in both countries continue to treat the site as a matter of sovereignty and pride.

## Domestic politics on both sides

The Preah Vihear dispute has often been shaped as much by internal politics as by geography.

In Thailand, the issue intersected with years of political conflict between royalist-nationalist “yellow shirt” movements, pro-Thaksin political forces, the military and elected governments. Opponents of Thai governments used the temple dispute to question the patriotism of officials seen as conciliatory toward Cambodia. The claim that leaders had compromised Thai territory became a powerful political weapon.

The Thai military also played a prominent role. Border disputes can strengthen the armed forces’ image as defenders of national sovereignty, especially during periods when civilian governments are under pressure. Even when leaders sought diplomatic solutions, they had to account for nationalist public opinion and military influence.

In Cambodia, Preah Vihear has served as a symbol of national unity and historical pride. Hun Sen’s government used the temple’s World Heritage recognition to bolster its legitimacy and portray itself as defender of Cambodian sovereignty. The dispute also allowed Phnom Penh to rally domestic support against a larger neighbor with which Cambodia has a complicated history.

For Cambodian leaders, Thailand’s claims over nearby land evoked memories of historical losses and foreign domination. For Thai nationalists, the ICJ ruling and UNESCO process became symbols of perceived diplomatic disadvantage and territorial vulnerability.

## Why the dispute is so difficult to resolve

Several factors have made Preah Vihear unusually sensitive:

1. **Colonial-era borders remain contested**  
   The frontier was shaped by old maps and treaties whose interpretation remains disputed.

2. **The temple and the surrounding land are legally distinct**  
   Cambodia’s sovereignty over the temple is internationally recognized, but some adjacent border areas have historically been less clearly demarcated.

3. **National identity is at stake**  
   Both countries see the site through the lens of history, pride and sovereignty.

4. **Domestic politics can inflame tensions**  
   Politicians and protest movements have used the issue to attack rivals.

5. **Military deployments create risk**  
   Even small incidents can escalate when troops are stationed close together in disputed terrain.

## A fragile calm

In recent years, Thailand and Cambodia have generally sought to manage the dispute through diplomacy, joint border mechanisms and efforts to avoid renewed fighting. Cross-border trade, tourism and regional cooperation give both sides strong incentives to prevent escalation.

Yet Preah Vihear remains a potent reminder that Southeast Asia’s borders are not merely lines on a map. They are tied to history, identity and political power. As long as parts of the frontier remain unsettled—and as long as nationalist politics can be mobilized around the temple—the area will retain the potential to become a military and diplomatic flashpoint.

For villagers living near the border, the issue is less abstract. Past clashes forced families into shelters, closed schools and disrupted livelihoods. Their experience underscores the human cost of a dispute in which ancient stones, modern borders and contemporary politics collide.

## Report: The July Cambodia–Thailand Temple Dispute Over Preah Vihear

### Overview

The July Cambodia–Thailand temple dispute centered on **Preah Vihear**, an ancient Hindu temple perched on a cliff in the Dangrek Mountains along the two countries’ border. Although the temple itself was awarded to Cambodia by the **International Court of Justice (ICJ) in 1962**, the surrounding land—especially an area of roughly **4.6 square kilometers** near the temple—remained contested.  

Tensions escalated sharply in July after Cambodia’s successful push to have Preah Vihear listed as a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**, a move that stirred nationalist feeling in both countries and triggered a military standoff near the border.

---

## Historical Background

Preah Vihear, known in Khmer as **Prasat Preah Vihear** and in Thai as **Phra Wihan**, dates mainly from the **11th and 12th centuries** and was built during the Khmer Empire. It is dedicated to the Hindu god Shiva and is architecturally significant for its dramatic north–south orientation along a mountain ridge.

The dispute has roots in colonial-era border mapping. In the early 20th century, French colonial authorities in Cambodia and Siam, now Thailand, produced maps that placed the temple on the Cambodian side of the frontier. Thailand later challenged this, arguing that the watershed line should determine the border and that the temple was naturally accessible from the Thai side.

In **1962**, the International Court of Justice ruled that the temple belonged to Cambodia. Thailand complied by withdrawing from the temple itself, but it did not accept Cambodian claims over some of the surrounding territory. The ICJ decision therefore settled ownership of the temple building but did not fully resolve the wider border demarcation.

---

## The July Flashpoint

The immediate trigger for the July crisis was Cambodia’s campaign to register Preah Vihear as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Cambodia saw the listing as a diplomatic and cultural victory, strengthening its international recognition of the temple’s heritage and sovereignty.

In Thailand, however, the issue became entangled in domestic politics. Critics accused the Thai government of conceding too much to Cambodia by supporting, or at least not blocking, the listing. Thai nationalist groups argued that Cambodia’s UNESCO bid could prejudice the unresolved border question and weaken Thailand’s claims to the disputed land around the temple.

As protests grew in Thailand, the issue moved from a heritage dispute into a matter of national pride and territorial sovereignty.

---

## Troop Redeployment and Military Standoff

In mid-July, tensions escalated when troops from both countries moved into the disputed border area near Preah Vihear. Cambodia said Thai soldiers had crossed into Cambodian territory near the temple. Thailand disputed this, saying its forces were on Thai soil or in an area whose sovereignty had not yet been settled.

Cambodia deployed soldiers around the temple and surrounding approaches, while Thailand reinforced its side of the border. The resulting standoff involved hundreds of troops, with both armies digging in near Buddhist pagodas, access roads, and strategic high ground close to the temple complex.

The most sensitive area was around a small pagoda near the disputed zone, often cited in reports at the time as a focal point of the confrontation. Cambodian authorities viewed the Thai military presence there as an incursion, while Thai officials described the land as still subject to bilateral demarcation.

Despite the buildup, both governments publicly stated that they wanted to avoid armed conflict. Military commanders held local-level talks, and diplomatic channels remained open. Still, the proximity of armed soldiers in a highly symbolic and disputed zone created a serious risk of accidental clashes.

---

## The Contested Land Around Preah Vihear

The core of the dispute was not the temple sanctuary itself, which international law recognized as Cambodian, but the surrounding land.

Cambodia argued that the 1962 ICJ ruling, together with colonial maps accepted in the case, supported its sovereignty over the temple vicinity. Cambodian officials maintained that Thai troops entering the area were violating Cambodian territory.

Thailand argued that the ICJ ruling applied only to the temple ruins and did not decide the status of the adjacent 4.6-square-kilometer zone. Thai officials emphasized that border demarcation remained incomplete and should be resolved through bilateral mechanisms rather than unilateral action by Cambodia or international bodies.

The terrain compounded the problem. Preah Vihear is easier to access from Thailand’s lower plains than from Cambodia’s steep cliff side. This geographic reality has long contributed to competing administrative, military, and emotional claims.

---

## Reactions in Cambodia

In Cambodia, the UNESCO listing was celebrated as a major national achievement. The government of Prime Minister **Hun Sen** presented the recognition as proof of Cambodia’s cultural prestige and territorial legitimacy. State media and public ceremonies framed Preah Vihear as a symbol of Khmer civilization and sovereignty.

The dispute also unfolded during a politically sensitive period in Cambodia, where national elections were approaching. The government’s firm stance against Thailand helped rally patriotic support. Cambodian leaders accused Thailand of violating Cambodian territory and warned that Cambodia would defend its sovereignty if necessary.

Public opinion in Cambodia was strongly nationalistic. Many Cambodians viewed Thai objections as a continuation of historical pressure from a larger neighbor. The temple became a rallying point for national unity, with widespread public anger over the presence of Thai troops near the site.

---

## Reactions in Thailand

In Thailand, the Preah Vihear issue became deeply tied to domestic political conflict. The government faced pressure from opposition forces and nationalist movements, especially groups that accused it of mishandling the UNESCO process and compromising Thai sovereignty.

Thai protesters argued that the government’s earlier support for Cambodia’s World Heritage application amounted to an unconstitutional or irresponsible concession. The issue was used by critics of the administration to mobilize public anger and challenge its legitimacy.

The Thai courts also became involved. Legal challenges over the government’s handling of the UNESCO listing intensified the political stakes, and Thai officials were forced to adopt a tougher public position. The dispute therefore reflected not only a border disagreement with Cambodia but also Thailand’s internal struggle between elected authorities, courts, royalist-nationalist groups, and street protest movements.

Many Thais saw the temple area as historically connected to Thailand because of geography, access routes, and local memory, even though the ICJ had ruled the temple itself belonged to Cambodia. Nationalist media coverage heightened public suspicion of Cambodian intentions.

---

## Diplomatic Efforts

Both sides sought to contain the crisis through talks. Defense and foreign ministry officials discussed troop redeployment, joint border mechanisms, and possible de-escalation measures. Cambodia also raised the possibility of involving international institutions if bilateral diplomacy failed, while Thailand preferred to keep the dispute within bilateral frameworks.

The Association of Southeast Asian Nations, ASEAN, watched the dispute with concern. The standoff was embarrassing for a region that emphasized peaceful cooperation and non-interference. However, ASEAN’s capacity to intervene directly was limited, particularly because both Cambodia and Thailand initially emphasized sovereign negotiation.

---

## Significance of the Dispute

The July standoff showed how unresolved border demarcation, colonial-era maps, domestic politics, and cultural heritage claims could combine into a dangerous crisis.

For Cambodia, Preah Vihear represented ancient Khmer glory, national sovereignty, and international recognition after decades of war and instability. For Thailand, the surrounding land became a symbol of territorial vigilance and a powerful tool in domestic political competition.

The dispute also demonstrated that UNESCO heritage listings can have geopolitical consequences when cultural sites sit on unresolved borders. What might have appeared to be a technical cultural designation became a trigger for military redeployment and nationalist mobilization.

---

## Conclusion

The July Cambodia–Thailand temple dispute was not simply about an ancient monument. It was about sovereignty, historical memory, domestic politics, and the unfinished business of border demarcation.

The temple of Preah Vihear itself had been legally recognized as Cambodian territory since 1962, but the land around it remained contested. Cambodia’s UNESCO success intensified Thai fears that the listing could strengthen Cambodian claims, while Cambodian leaders saw Thai troop movements as a direct challenge to their sovereignty.

Troop redeployments on both sides turned the dispute into a tense military standoff, though both governments initially sought to avoid open conflict. Public reactions in Cambodia and Thailand were deeply nationalistic, shaped by historical grievances and contemporary political pressures.

The July crisis became one of the most serious Cambodia–Thailand confrontations of the period and foreshadowed further tensions along the border in the years that followed.
